name: Osun Printed Banded-Collar Shirt
description:
A short-sleeve button-front shirt with a banded (mandarin) collar and a West African-inspired geometric print — deep indigo and burnt sienna on a cream ground, with a repeating angular motif that references Yoruba textile traditions while feeling entirely contemporary. Made by Osun Workshop, a small-batch label run out of a Tier 3 residential block in the Chicago south corridor by a second-generation textile designer. The fabric is a medium-weight linen-cotton blend that breathes in humid summers and holds its shape after hand washing.

Each run of prints is different — Osun releases maybe four patterns a year, and once they're gone, they're gone. The shirts have become a quiet status marker in certain creative and professional circles: not flashy, but specific. You either know Osun or you don't.
what_it_says: You have taste that runs deeper than a corporate catalog, and you support independent makers when you can afford to.
story_hooks: A specific Osun print — a limited run of 40 shirts — was worn by several attendees at a protest that turned violent. The print has since become associated with the event, and wearing it now carries unintended political weight.
The designer behind Osun has received a buyout offer from a Tier 4 corponation that wants to scale the brand. Regulars are watching to see if she takes it.

A fake Osun shirt has appeared on the market — close enough to fool most people, but the print is slightly wrong in a way that experts can spot. Someone is trying to understand who's buying the real ones.
